[] Ah, sí, many times across the centuries, long before the notion of 'book clubs' took root in parlors. In the courtyards of colonial Mexico, for example, evenings would soften into shadows as neighbors gathered under the jacaranda trees, not for any scheduled society, but simply because the air was warm and the stories were waiting. Someone would read aloud from a tattered chapbook while others embroidered, prepared tamales, or cradled sleepy children—no secretary to take minutes, no rules to follow, only the ebb and flow of voices.

In 18th-century Spain, there were the *tertulias*, which could be formal in the salons of the nobility, but also spilled into café corners where a wandering poet might recite verses to listeners who happened to pass by. And still earlier, in indigenous pueblos of the Southwest, the telling of history was braided into song, dance, and the flicker of firelight—participants shifting between teller and listener without ceremony.

What unites all of these moments is that they lived outside the strict geometry of an organized group. The magic of shared narrative, *la magia de la palabra*, was born from spontaneity and mutual affection, not agendas. Sometimes I think those are the purest gatherings—when people meet not because the calendar insists, but because the heart compels them to listen and speak.
